title: SN2: hydrosulfide and iodomethane

steps.name: One concerted step
steps.say: A lone pair on sulfur attacks carbon from the side opposite iodine. As the S-C bond forms, the C-I bond breaks and its electrons leave with iodine.
steps.why: {{HS-}} is electron rich and one of the best nucleophiles in the lecture table (126,000). The carbon of {{CH3I}} is electron poor ({{d+}}) and unhindered, and iodide is a weak base, so a good leaving group. Both species are in the transition state: rate = k[{{HS-}}][{{CH3I}}].
hints: Which atom has a lone pair and a negative charge?
The nucleophile's pair goes to the carbon that carries the leaving group.
Two arrows: S lone pair to C, then the C-I bond to I.

takeaway: SN2 is one step with two arrows: nucleophile in from the back, leaving group out the front. No intermediate.

title: E2: tert-butyl bromide and hydroxide

steps.name: One concerted step
steps.say: Hydroxide takes a hydrogen from the carbon next to the C-Br carbon. The C-H electrons swing in to make the pi bond, and bromide leaves, all at once.
steps.why: The carbon is tertiary, so the backside is blocked and SN2 cannot happen. Hydroxide is a strong base, so it does not wait for the bromide to ionize: it removes a beta hydrogen that is anti to the bromine. rate = k[RBr][{{HO-}}].
hints: A strong base takes a proton. Which protons sit on a carbon next to the C-Br carbon?
The electrons of that C-H bond cannot just disappear: they become the new C=C.
Three arrows: O lone pair to H, C-H bond to C-C, C-Br bond to Br.

takeaway: E2 is one step with three arrows: base to H, C-H to the new pi bond, C-LG to the leaving group. H and LG are anti-periplanar.

title: SN1: tert-butyl bromide in water

steps.name: Ionization (rate-determining)
steps.say: The C-Br bond breaks by itself. Both electrons leave with bromine, and a tertiary carbocation is left behind.
steps.why: Three methyl groups stabilize the positive carbon, and water, a polar protic solvent, stabilizes both ions. This slow step involves only the alkyl halide: rate = k[RBr].
hints: No nucleophile takes part in the first step.
Break the C-Br bond: which atom keeps the electrons?

steps.name: Water attacks the carbocation
steps.say: A lone pair on water's oxygen attacks the flat, positive carbon. Oxygen now has three bonds and a positive charge.
steps.why: The carbocation is a strong electrophile, so even a poor nucleophile like water reacts quickly. It can attack either face of the planar carbon, which is why SN1 at a stereocentre gives a racemic mixture.
hints: The carbocation is electron poor. What nearby has a lone pair?

steps.name: A second water removes the proton
steps.say: Another water molecule takes one hydrogen from the positively charged oxygen. The O-H electrons stay on oxygen, which becomes neutral.
steps.why: A protonated alcohol is a strong acid ({{pKa}} about −2), so the solvent removes the proton. Do not forget this step: the product is the alcohol, not its conjugate acid.
hints: The oxygen is positive and still has two hydrogens: one must go.
Two arrows: water's lone pair to H, then the O-H bond to O.

takeaway: SN1 with a neutral nucleophile is three steps: leaving group leaves, nucleophile attacks, proton comes off. The first step is the slow one.

title: E1: tert-butyl bromide in hot water

steps.name: Ionization (rate-determining)
steps.say: The same first step as SN1: the C-Br bond breaks and leaves the tertiary carbocation.
steps.why: SN1 and E1 share this carbocation. What happens to it next decides the product.
hints: It starts exactly like SN1.

steps.name: Water removes a beta hydrogen
steps.say: Water acts as a base: it takes a hydrogen from a carbon next to the positive carbon, and the C-H electrons form the C=C.
steps.why: A hydrogen next to a carbocation is acidic, so a weak base is enough. Elimination makes two particles from one, so it is favoured by entropy and wins at higher temperature.
hints: Water is the only base in the flask.
Take an H from a CH3, not from the positive carbon itself (it has none).

takeaway: E1 is two steps: leaving group leaves, then a weak base removes a neighbouring hydrogen. Same carbocation as SN1.

title: A Grignard reagent and carbon dioxide

steps.name: The carbanion-like carbon attacks carbon dioxide
steps.say: The electrons of the C-Mg bond attack the carbon of carbon dioxide. To keep that carbon at four bonds, one C=O pi bond's electrons move up onto oxygen.
steps.why: Carbon bonded to magnesium is strongly {{d-}}: the reagent behaves as a carbanion, R:⁻. The carbon of {{CO2}} is electron poor because two oxygens pull on it. Electron rich attacks electron poor.
hints: Where are the electrons in a Grignard reagent? Think of it as R:⁻ and ⁺MgBr.
Which atom of O=C=O is electron poor?
Two arrows: C-Mg bond to the CO2 carbon, and one C=O pi bond onto O.

steps.name: Acid workup protonates the carboxylate
steps.say: In the second, separate step, acid is added. A lone pair on the negative oxygen takes a proton from {{H3O+}}.
steps.why: The acid must come after the first step. If it were present at the start it would destroy the Grignard reagent, which is a very strong base. A carboxylate ({{pKa}} of the acid about 4) is easily protonated by {{H3O+}} ({{pKa}} −1.5).
hints: The product is the neutral acid, so the O⁻ needs a proton.
Two arrows: O lone pair to H, then the H-O bond onto water's oxygen.

takeaway: A Grignard reagent is R:⁻. It attacks the electron-poor carbon of whatever it meets, and acid is added only afterwards.

title: Methyllithium and water: an acid-base reaction

steps.name: Proton transfer
steps.say: The electrons of the C-Li bond take a hydrogen from water. The H-O electrons stay on oxygen as hydroxide.
steps.why: Water ({{pKa}} 15.7) is a far stronger acid than methane ({{pKa}} 50 to 60), so the equilibrium lies completely on the side of methane. This is why organolithium and Grignard reagents must be kept away from water and alcohols.
hints: Treat C-Li as a carbanion: which hydrogen nearby is acidic?
Two arrows: C-Li bond to H, H-O bond to O.

takeaway: Organometallic reagents are very strong bases: any O-H or N-H protonates them. With {{D2O}} the carbon picks up D instead.
